summary: Reports on an ad hoc workshop on middleware held at the International Center for Advanced Internet Research in December 1998. It records the need for a better framework for middleware research and a list of topics needing more work. This is an informational memo.

eli5.summary: Some experts met to talk about the software glue between programs and wrote down what to work on next.

why do advanced applications need middleware
how does policy management work in middleware
what is a policy decision point
subtitle: Report on middleware requirements and architecture for advanced network applications.

tldr.problem: Advanced network applications (distributed computing, digital libraries, video services, research tools) need capabilities beyond what TCP/IP provides, but there is no agreed-upon set of services and standards to build this middleware layer.
tldr.mechanism: A workshop of researchers and practitioners identified that middleware is an unstructured collection of services between transport (TCP/IP) and application APIs. The report catalogs core components like authentication, policy management, directories, resource discovery, and quality of service, then maps how they interact and where further development is needed.
tldr.outcome: The report identifies a research agenda for middleware, emphasizing the need for unified frameworks around policy definition languages, directory services, AAA infrastructure, and resource management to enable next-generation distributed applications.

facts.label: Workshop location
facts.value: International Center for Advanced Internet Research (ICAIR)

today: RFC 2768 is an Informational document reporting on a workshop held in December 1998. Many of the middleware initiatives it discusses have evolved: AAA protocols and standards have advanced significantly, policy frameworks have seen adoption, directory services are widely deployed, and Grid computing has matured into cloud computing. However, the fundamental challenge of integrating these disparate components remains relevant.

sections.title: What Is Middleware?
sections.content:
Middleware sits between the network transport (TCP/IP) and the applications that use it. It is the collection of services that programs need to function well in a networked environment: ways to find resources, prove identity, control access, manage quality of service, schedule work, and handle data across multiple machines.

The workshop participants quickly found that there is no single definition of middleware because it depends on perspective. Application developers see everything below their API as middleware. Network engineers see anything above IP as middleware. Distributed systems builders see it somewhere between TCP and APIs, often divided into application-specific upper middleware, generic middle middleware, and resource-specific lower middleware.

The rough consensus was to define middleware as those services found above the transport layer but below application-level APIs. The report emphasizes that middleware often extends beyond the network itself into compute, storage, and other resources the network connects.
sections.eli5: Middleware is the software between what networks do and what programs ask for. Different people call different things middleware depending on their job.

sections.title: Why Advanced Applications Need Middleware
sections.content:
The applications driving middleware requirements are cutting-edge: distributed computing on national networks, virtual reality with haptics and live interaction (teleimmersion), high-rate scientific instruments sending 60+ MB/s of data, collaborative research across institutions, digital libraries and data archives, and computational Grids. These differ fundamentally from web browsing.

A teleimmersion application, for example, needs multiple independent network channels simultaneously, each with its own latency, jitter, bandwidth, and burst tolerance, all coordinated through a single middleware interface. Scientific instruments need to steer devices based on real-time analysis of incoming data, requiring high bandwidth, low latency, and security all managed together. These requirements cannot be met by generic TCP/IP alone.

Similarly, researchers also emphasized the need for pass-through services: the ability to bypass middleware and directly access the operating system or network when needed, even while leveraging middleware for other aspects of the application.
sections.eli5: New science and research programs need to move huge amounts of data, coordinate many computers together, and react in real time. The internet was not designed for these uses, so they need custom software on top.

sections.title: Core Middleware Components
sections.content:
The workshop identified exemplary middleware services worth standardizing. APIs and Signaling let applications request resources (network quality, priority, bandwidth) without learning multiple interfaces. Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) establish identity, determine permissions, and log resource use. AAA is complicated by distributed scenarios where one program might need to act on behalf of another across multiple administrative domains.

Policy is integral to all middleware. Policies, expressed as if condition then action rules, link business requirements (such as service-level agreements) to device implementation. Policy management requires policy decision points (PDPs) that make decisions and policy enforcement points (PEPs) that carry them out.

Directories store and retrieve data about resources, services, policies, and users. Unlike databases, directories are optimized for high read rates, offer per-attribute access control, and use containment to organize information hierarchically. Resource Management handles discovery, allocation, and scheduling of network and compute resources. Quality of Service (QoS)** provides bandwidth, latency, and loss guarantees for different traffic types.
sections.eli5: Middleware needs to let programs ask for what they need, prove who they are, store information about resources, find those resources, and promise to deliver certain speeds. Each is a big piece of work.

sections.title: Integration and Standards Challenges
sections.content:
The workshop consensus was that middleware is not hierarchical or layered in a traditional sense. Rather, it is an unstructured, often orthogonal collection of components that applications use individually or in combination. This approach avoided unproductive theoretical debates and let the group focus on practical needs.

However, integration challenges remain significant. Policy requires AAA functions to establish trust. Directories store policy information and resource metadata. API frameworks must unify access to these services so developers do not learn separate interfaces for each middleware capability. Currently, multiple policy definition languages exist (RPSL, RPCL, SPSL, PFDL, PAX, Keynote) in the IETF, and similar languages exist in distributed computing projects (Globus uses RSL; Condor uses matchmaking bidding). The workshop noted that these should eventually be merged into a coherent specification.

Another architectural issue is the need for a distributed, replicated database service that combines the best of directories and relational databases: high read performance, transactional integrity, complex queries, and hierarchical organization. No general middleware component provides this today.
sections.eli5: All these pieces need to work together, but they were designed separately. The challenge is making them talk to each other without forcing developers to learn too many different ways of asking for the same things.

sections.title: Organizational and Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
The workshop noted that middleware development is distributed across many communities: the IETF (standards for protocols and information models), the DMTF (desktop management and information models), the Grid Forum (distributed computing), Internet2 and the Next Generation Internet (NGI) initiative (advanced networking), and academic research groups. Different communities develop overlapping technologies (e.g., policy models) without always coordinating.

The report emphasizes that middleware standards and protocols are meaningless without supporting infrastructure. DNS is valuable only because a system of DNS servers and name registries exists. Similarly, PKI requires certificate authorities and key distribution infrastructure. New middleware services like distributed resource management, policy enforcement, and advanced authentication will require extensive administrative and operational infrastructure to become useful.

Future advanced applications will require multiple PDPs managing different resource types (QoS, security, storage, proxy agents, online facilities). A general model is needed to define protocols and mechanisms for cooperating PDPs from different domains and resource genres. For policies to be implemented coherently, the system must discover and track resources and their utilization.
sections.eli5: Many organizations are building different parts of middleware, but they don't always talk to each other. For middleware to actually work, it needs servers, administrators, and infrastructure just like the network itself.
